questions.stem:
In an enzyme assay, purified HIV reverse transcriptase copies an RNA template into DNA. Drug X is added. Drug X does not need to be phosphorylated inside cells, is not incorporated into the growing DNA strand, and binds a hydrophobic pocket on the enzyme separate from the site where nucleotides bind. Raising the concentration of natural deoxynucleotides does not overcome the inhibition.

Drug X is most likely which of the following?
choices: Tenofovir
Abacavir
Stavudine
Doravirine
Maraviroc

explain.html:
Reverse transcription, the conversion of viral RNA to DNA, is the target of two classes. NRTIs (abacavir, emtricitabine, lamivudine, tenofovir, zidovudine, didanosine, stavudine) stop that conversion through competitive inhibition with the natural nucleotides, so adding more substrate competes the drug off. NNRTIs (efavirenz, nevirapine, etravirine, rilpivirine, doravirine) use allosteric inhibition: they bind an alternative binding site on the enzyme, so extra substrate does not overcome them.

Drug X binds a pocket separate from the nucleotide site and is not overcome by raising deoxynucleotide levels, which is the NNRTI pattern. Of the choices, only doravirine is an NNRTI. The distinction matters clinically because the two classes have different toxicity and interaction profiles, and they are combined rather than substituted for one another.
explain.table:
NRTINNRTI
MechanismCompetitive inhibitionAllosteric inhibition (alternative site)
MembersAbacavir, emtricitabine, lamivudine, tenofovir, zidovudineEfavirenz, nevirapine, etravirine, rilpivirine, doravirine
Class toxicityMitochondrial: lactic acidosis, steatosis, neuropathy, lipoatrophyRash including SJS/TEN, hepatotoxicity
Drug interactionsMinimal; most need renal dose adjustmentCYP3A4 inducers (not rilpivirine or doravirine); no renal adjustment
why: Tenofovir is an NRTI, so it competes with natural nucleotides and would be overcome by more substrate.
Abacavir is an NRTI that acts by competitive inhibition.
Stavudine is an NRTI that acts by competitive inhibition.
Maraviroc blocks the CCR5 coreceptor at entry and does not act on reverse transcriptase.
explain.takeaway: NRTIs competitively inhibit reverse transcriptase, while NNRTIs such as doravirine bind an alternative allosteric site and are not overcome by substrate.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify drug classes of antiretrovirals and understand their mechanisms of action

rows.why: Abacavir is an NRTI that acts by competitive inhibition.
rows.if_right: a competitive inhibitor that requires HLA-B*5701 testing before use

rows.why: Stavudine is an NRTI that acts by competitive inhibition.
rows.if_right: a competitive inhibitor with the highest risk of mitochondrial toxicity and lipoatrophy

questions.stem:
A 33-year-old man of Scandinavian descent with newly diagnosed HIV infection is choosing a single-tablet regimen. His physician favors a tablet containing dolutegravir, abacavir, and lamivudine. Baseline results show plasma HIV RNA 42,000 copies/mL, CD4 count 510/mm3, normal kidney function, negative hepatitis B serologies, and a wild-type genotype. One pharmacogenetic test was also sent and returns positive.

Which of the following is the most appropriate action regarding this regimen?
choices: Start it, because his kidney function is normal
Start it but reduce the abacavir dose
Start it with a low-dose test challenge
Avoid abacavir because of hypersensitivity risk
Avoid lamivudine because of the risk of a hepatitis B flare

explain.html:
Abacavir requires HLA-B*5701 testing before use. If the test is positive, abacavir is contraindicated because of an increased risk of hypersensitivity reaction, and a patient with a past reaction should not be rechallenged. The allele has an overall prevalence of 3 to 5% and the highest risk in Scandinavian men. Other abacavir points: no renal adjustment is needed, alcohol increases exposure, and efficacy may be diminished with an initial viral load above 100,000 copies/mL.

This Scandinavian man's pharmacogenetic test is positive, so the dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine tablet must be avoided. His normal kidney function is beside the point, since abacavir needs no renal adjustment. A regimen without abacavir, such as bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide, fits his other results.
why: Kidney function is irrelevant to this decision, since abacavir needs no renal adjustment.
A positive test is a contraindication, and a lower dose does not remove the hypersensitivity risk.
Re-challenge is not recommended, and a positive allele contraindicates abacavir outright.
Lamivudine's flare risk applies only when stopping it in hepatitis B coinfection, and his serologies are negative.
explain.takeaway: A positive HLA-B*5701 test contraindicates abacavir because of hypersensitivity risk, and a patient who has reacted should never be rechallenged.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify administration considerations, adverse effects, and drug interactions for antiretrovirals

questions.stem:
A 36-year-old woman with long-standing HIV infection was switched to an older regimen 3 months ago because of drug interactions with her other medications. She now reports fatigue and exertional dyspnea, and she notes darkening of her fingernails. She also has proximal muscle aching.

[[labs 0]]

The drug responsible for these findings is also used for which of the following purposes?
choices: Boosting protease inhibitor levels
Long-acting injectable pre-exposure prophylaxis
Treatment of chronic hepatitis B infection
Salvage therapy for multidrug-resistant virus in adults
Preventing mother-to-child transmission at delivery

explain.html:
Zidovudine (AZT) is an older NRTI with a recognizable adverse effect list: macrocytic anemia, myopathy, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, headache, insomnia, nail pigmentation, lipoatrophy and hyperlipidemia. It is renally eliminated and has minimal drug interactions. It comes in oral and IV formulations, and that is the reason it is still used: it is given during childbirth and to the infant to prevent mother-to-child transmission.

This woman developed a macrocytic anemia with normal B12 and folate, proximal muscle aching and darkened nails after switching to an older regimen, which points to zidovudine. The same drug's IV form is what is used at delivery.
explain.table:
NRTISignature adverse effects or uses
ZidovudineMacrocytic anemia, myopathy, nail pigmentation; used at delivery and in the infant
Tenofovir DFRenal toxicity, Fanconi syndrome, decreased bone density; HBV activity
Tenofovir AFLess renal and bone effect than TDF; increased lipids; HBV activity
AbacavirHypersensitivity in HLA-B*5701 carriers
Lamivudine, emtricitabineWell tolerated; HBV flare if stopped
why: Boosting is done with ritonavir or cobicistat, which inhibit CYP3A4.
Long-acting injectable PrEP uses cabotegravir or lenacapavir.
Zidovudine has no hepatitis B activity; tenofovir, emtricitabine and lamivudine do.
Salvage agents for multidrug-resistant virus include enfuvirtide, ibalizumab, fostemsavir and lenacapavir.
explain.takeaway: Zidovudine causes macrocytic anemia, myopathy and nail pigmentation, and its IV form is still given during childbirth and to the infant to prevent perinatal transmission.
explain.topic: Zidovudine adverse effects and perinatal use
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify administration considerations, adverse effects, and drug interactions for antiretrovirals

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old woman has taken an antiretroviral regimen containing stavudine and didanosine for many years in a resource-limited setting. Over several weeks she develops nausea, abdominal pain, and fatigue, along with burning numbness of both feet and hands in a glove-and-stocking pattern. Her liver is enlarged. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.28 with a low bicarbonate, serum lactate is 7.5 mmol/L (normal less than 2), and ultrasound shows fatty infiltration of the liver. She has lost fat from her face and limbs.

These adverse effects are best explained by inhibition of which of the following?
choices: Hepatic CYP3A4
Mitochondrial DNA polymerase
Viral integrase
Renal tubular creatinine secretion
Host UGT1A1 glucuronidation

explain.html:
The NRTI class carries a boxed warning for mitochondrial toxicity. Its long-term picture is lactic acidosis (acidosis, ketosis, hyperglycemia, fatty liver), severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, and peripheral neuropathy in a gloving pattern, with lipoatrophy as a related effect. The risk is higher with didanosine and stavudine, and lipoatrophy runs stavudine, then zidovudine, then the other NRTIs. Because the NRTIs are nucleoside analogs, they can interfere with the host's own mitochondrial DNA synthesis, which is the basis of this class toxicity.

This woman took stavudine and didanosine for years and now has a lactate of 7.5 with acidemia, an enlarged fatty liver, glove-and-stocking neuropathy and facial and limb fat loss. Every feature belongs to NRTI mitochondrial toxicity, which is why these two drugs have fallen out of use.
why: CYP3A4 inhibition produces drug interactions, the property ritonavir and cobicistat are used for.
Integrase is the target of INSTIs, whose class effects are weight gain and creatine kinase elevation.
Blocking tubular creatinine secretion raises creatinine without injury, as with cobicistat.
UGT1A1 glucuronidation is how most integrase inhibitors are metabolized, not the cause of NRTI toxicity.
explain.takeaway: NRTI class toxicity is mitochondrial (lactic acidosis, hepatic steatosis, peripheral neuropathy, lipoatrophy), with the highest risk from didanosine and stavudine.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify administration considerations, adverse effects, and drug interactions for antiretrovirals

rows.if_right: a patient on a boosted protease inhibitor with rising levels of a co-administered drug

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old man started a once-daily single tablet for HIV 2 weeks ago and takes it with breakfast. He reports vivid, disturbing dreams, dizziness, trouble concentrating at work, and feeling low in mood. A urine drug screen done for a new job was positive for cannabinoids, although he denies any use. His tablet contains two NRTIs plus one drug from another class.

Which of the following is the most appropriate advice regarding how he takes the responsible drug?
choices: Take it at bedtime on an empty stomach
Take it with a 500-calorie meal each morning
Separate it from calcium supplements by several hours
Take it with a proton pump inhibitor to aid absorption
Double the dose so the effects resolve sooner

explain.html:
Efavirenz is the NNRTI known for CNS effects: impaired concentration, abnormal dreams, confusion and dizziness, with warnings for serious neuropsychiatric symptoms (depression, suicidal ideation), convulsions, QT prolongation, hepatotoxicity and elevated triglycerides. It can cause a false positive for cannabinoid and benzodiazepine drug screens. Taking it with food raises the peak concentration, which worsens side effects without improving efficacy, so it is taken at bedtime on an empty stomach.

This man takes a two-NRTI-plus-one tablet with breakfast and has vivid dreams, dizziness, poor concentration, low mood and an unexplained positive cannabinoid screen. That is efavirenz taken the wrong way, and moving the dose to bedtime on an empty stomach lowers the CNS effects. His mood still needs close follow-up given the neuropsychiatric warning.
explain.table:
NNRTIHow to takeKey points
EfavirenzBedtime, empty stomachCNS effects, false-positive cannabinoid screen, CYP inducer
RilpivirineWith food (about 500 kcal)Needs acid: PPIs contraindicated; avoid with VL above 100,000 or CD4 below 200
DoravirineNot specifiedWell tolerated; high genetic barrier to resistance
why: A meal raises efavirenz levels and side effects; taking it with food is the rule for rilpivirine.
Separating from calcium is advice for integrase inhibitors, which chelate polyvalent cations.
Acid suppression does not help efavirenz, and PPIs are contraindicated with rilpivirine.
A higher dose would raise levels and worsen the concentration-dependent CNS effects.
explain.takeaway: Efavirenz causes CNS and neuropsychiatric effects and false-positive cannabinoid screens, and it is taken at bedtime on an empty stomach to limit them.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify administration considerations, adverse effects, and drug interactions for antiretrovirals

questions.stem:
A 47-year-old woman with HIV has had an undetectable viral load for 4 years on rilpivirine, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide, taken daily with dinner. Three months ago a new physician started her on daily omeprazole for reflux symptoms. Her adherence is excellent by pharmacy refill records. Her plasma HIV RNA is now 6,800 copies/mL.

Which of the following best explains her loss of viral suppression?
choices: Omeprazole induced CYP3A4 metabolism of tenofovir
Rilpivirine requires gastric acid for absorption
Omeprazole chelated rilpivirine in the gut lumen
Taking rilpivirine with food prevented its absorption
Emtricitabine was antagonized by the newly added drug

explain.html:
Rilpivirine is an NNRTI that is taken with food, ideally a 500-calorie meal, because acid is needed for its absorption. That makes acid suppression its key interaction: proton pump inhibitors are contraindicated (pantoprazole, omeprazole), and H2-receptor antagonists such as famotidine must be separated in time. It is also a CYP3A4 substrate, so strong inducers such as rifampin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital and St. John's wort are contraindicated.

This woman was suppressed for 4 years on rilpivirine/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide taken with dinner, with excellent adherence, until daily omeprazole was added. Raising her gastric pH dropped rilpivirine absorption, weakening the regimen enough for virus to return. The fix is to remove the PPI or change the regimen, with resistance testing since the virus replicated on partial drug levels.
why: Tenofovir is not cleared through CYP3A4, and omeprazole is not acting as an inducer here.
Chelation is the interaction between integrase inhibitors and polyvalent cations.
Rilpivirine should be taken with food, which helps its absorption.
The antagonistic interaction is between emtricitabine and lamivudine, not with omeprazole.
explain.takeaway: Rilpivirine needs gastric acid for absorption and is taken with food, so proton pump inhibitors are contraindicated and can cause virologic failure.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify administration considerations, adverse effects, and drug interactions for antiretrovirals

rows.if_right: an integrase inhibitor taken at the same time as calcium, magnesium or aluminum

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old woman with HIV has had an undetectable viral load for 3 years on dolutegravir plus two NRTIs, taken each morning on an empty stomach. Six months ago she was diagnosed with osteoporosis and began taking a calcium carbonate supplement and a multivitamin with iron every morning together with her antiretroviral pills. She also uses an aluminum-magnesium antacid for heartburn. Her viral load is now 1,900 copies/mL.

Which of the following is the most appropriate change?
choices: Stop dolutegravir and add a protease inhibitor without a booster
Separate the supplements from dolutegravir or take them with food
Add a proton pump inhibitor to replace the antacid and continue the supplements
Increase the calcium dose, because dolutegravir causes bone loss
Switch dolutegravir to raltegravir, which does not interact with cations

explain.html:
Integrase inhibitors (bictegravir, cabotegravir, dolutegravir, elvitegravir, raltegravir) are potent, generally well tolerated, and mostly metabolized by UGT1A1. Their major interaction is a chelating complex with polyvalent cations: aluminum, calcium and magnesium, found in multivitamins, aluminum- and magnesium-containing antacids such as Maalox, and calcium supplements. The fix is to separate the products or take them together with food. Because this is a class effect, switching to another INSTI does not avoid it.

This woman was suppressed for 3 years on dolutegravir until she began calcium, a multivitamin and an aluminum-magnesium antacid taken at the same time as her pills on an empty stomach. Chelation lowered dolutegravir absorption and her viral load rose to 1,900 copies/mL. Spacing the supplements or taking everything with food restores absorption.
explain.table:
InteractionAffected drug or classManagement
Polyvalent cations (Ca, Mg, Al)All integrase inhibitorsSeparate, or take together with food
Acid suppression (PPI)RilpivirinePPI contraindicated; separate H2RA
Estrogen contraceptionNNRTI inducers (efavirenz)Progestin-only method or copper IUD
why: Protease inhibitors are given boosted, unboosted darunavir is not recommended, and this interaction is fixable.
PPIs matter for rilpivirine, and continuing simultaneous calcium still blocks dolutegravir.
More simultaneous calcium would lower dolutegravir absorption further, and bone loss is a tenofovir DF effect.
Chelation is a class effect of all integrase inhibitors, raltegravir included.
explain.takeaway: All integrase inhibitors chelate polyvalent cations such as calcium, magnesium and aluminum, so these products are separated from the INSTI or taken together with food.
explain.topic: Integrase inhibitor chelation with polyvalent cations
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify administration considerations, adverse effects, and drug interactions for antiretrovirals

questions.stem:
A 39-year-old man with HIV and normal kidney function switches to a single tablet containing elvitegravir, cobicistat, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide. Two weeks later his serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.1 mg/dL. Urinalysis is normal, with no protein or glucose. A measured glomerular filtration rate using an exogenous marker is unchanged from before the switch.

Which of the following best explains the rise in creatinine?
choices: Acute tubular necrosis from tenofovir
Proximal tubular Fanconi syndrome
Inhibition of tubular creatinine secretion
Rhabdomyolysis from the integrase drug
Prerenal azotemia from volume depletion

explain.html:
Two drugs are used as pharmacokinetic boosters. Ritonavir has antiviral activity but is used at low dose to inhibit CYP3A4. Cobicistat has no antiviral activity and is a CYP3A4 inhibitor used to boost elvitegravir or a protease inhibitor. Its listed adverse effect is an increase in serum creatinine due to inhibition of creatinine excretion, with no effect on GFR. Bictegravir is similarly listed with a small rise in serum creatinine (0.1 to 0.2 mg/dL) when therapy starts.

This man switched to elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide and his creatinine rose from 0.9 to 1.1 mg/dL. His urinalysis is normal and a measured GFR is unchanged, so his kidneys are filtering normally. The rise reflects blocked tubular creatinine secretion, not kidney injury, and it does not require stopping the drug.
explain.table:
RitonavirCobicistat
Antiviral activityYes, but not used as a single PINone
Mechanism as boosterCYP3A4 inhibitorCYP3A4 inhibitor
Adverse effectsGI upset, loss of appetite, dyslipidemia, paresthesiasRaised serum creatinine with no effect on GFR
why: Tubular necrosis would lower GFR and usually change the urinalysis.
Fanconi syndrome causes glycosuria and proteinuria, which are absent, and is linked to tenofovir DF.
Rhabdomyolysis would bring muscle symptoms and is tied mainly to raltegravir.
Prerenal azotemia lowers GFR and follows volume loss, which he has not had.
explain.takeaway: Cobicistat raises serum creatinine by inhibiting tubular creatinine secretion without changing the true glomerular filtration rate.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify administration considerations, adverse effects, and drug interactions for antiretrovirals

questions.stem:
A 44-year-old man is prescribed darunavir taken together with a low dose of ritonavir. He asks why he needs a second protease inhibitor. His physician explains that at this low dose ritonavir contributes little antiviral effect, and that ritonavir was historically used at full doses as an antiviral but was poorly tolerated.

Which of the following best describes the purpose of low-dose ritonavir in this regimen?
choices: It inhibits CYP3A4, raising darunavir levels
It induces CYP3A4, shortening darunavir's half-life
It blocks CCR5 so darunavir can enter cells
It chelates cations that would bind darunavir
It prevents the hyperlipidemia caused by darunavir

explain.html:
Protease inhibitors are CYP3A4 substrates, and many are also inhibitors, so they are given boosted to increase their concentrations. Ritonavir has antiviral activity but should not be used as a single PI; at full doses it was historically very poorly tolerated. Today it is a CYP3A4 inhibitor used to boost other PIs by inhibiting their metabolism. Cobicistat does the same job with no antiviral activity. Unboosted darunavir is on the list of regimens not recommended.

This man takes darunavir with low-dose ritonavir, and the ritonavir's purpose is to slow darunavir's metabolism so it reaches effective levels. The price is that boosted regimens carry many drug interactions, and ritonavir adds GI effects, loss of appetite, dyslipidemia and paresthesias.
why: Induction would lower darunavir levels, the opposite of boosting.
Maraviroc is the drug that blocks CCR5, and ritonavir does not act at entry.
Chelation by polyvalent cations is an integrase inhibitor problem, not a protease inhibitor one.
Ritonavir itself causes dyslipidemia, and darunavir's hyperlipidemia needs monitoring.
explain.takeaway: Low-dose ritonavir boosts protease inhibitors by inhibiting CYP3A4, raising their levels at the cost of many drug interactions.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify administration considerations, adverse effects, and drug interactions for antiretrovirals

rows.if_right: a drug that binds a host chemokine receptor and requires a tropism test

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old man with HIV started a boosted protease inhibitor with two NRTIs 6 weeks ago. He feels well, but a coworker noticed that the whites of his eyes look yellow. He has no abdominal pain, and his urine is normal in color.

[[labs 0]]

Which protease inhibitor is he most likely taking?
choices: Darunavir
Atazanavir
Lopinavir
Fosamprenavir
Tipranavir

explain.html:
Protease inhibitors share class effects: lipodystrophy, GI upset, hepatotoxicity, and metabolic issues (dyslipidemia and insulin resistance), plus CYP3A4 interactions. Individual PIs have signatures. Atazanavir is taken with food, is lipid neutral with a low association with lipodystrophy, commonly causes asymptomatic hyperbilirubinemia, and can cause nephrolithiasis. Darunavir causes hyperlipidemia and may cause rash (it contains a sulfa moiety). Lopinavir/ritonavir commonly causes GI intolerance and can cause pancreatitis.

This man has scleral icterus 6 weeks into a boosted PI regimen, with an elevated indirect bilirubin, normal liver enzymes and no hemolysis. An isolated, asymptomatic hyperbilirubinemia is the atazanavir signature, and it is not a sign of liver injury.
explain.table:
Protease inhibitorSignature effectsNotes
AtazanavirAsymptomatic hyperbilirubinemia, nephrolithiasis; lipid neutralTake with food; acid suppressors interact
DarunavirHyperlipidemia, rashSulfa moiety; methadone interaction
Lopinavir/ritonavirGI intolerance, pancreatitisOnly PI co-formulated with ritonavir
why: Darunavir is linked to hyperlipidemia and rash, not isolated hyperbilirubinemia.
Lopinavir/ritonavir mainly causes GI intolerance and can cause pancreatitis.
Fosamprenavir is a protease inhibitor without the unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that marks atazanavir.
Tipranavir is a protease inhibitor without the unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that marks atazanavir.
explain.takeaway: Atazanavir commonly causes benign, asymptomatic hyperbilirubinemia, while protease inhibitors as a class cause dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, lipodystrophy and GI upset.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify administration considerations, adverse effects, and drug interactions for antiretrovirals

questions.stem:
A 49-year-old woman with multidrug-resistant HIV is started on a salvage drug given by twice-daily subcutaneous injection. The drug is a peptide that binds the viral transmembrane envelope protein and prevents it from folding into the conformation that brings viral and host membranes together. Within weeks nearly every injection site develops a painful nodule.

Which other risk is specifically associated with this drug?
choices: Macrocytic anemia
Bacterial pneumonia
Fanconi syndrome
Hyperbilirubinemia
Neural tube defects

explain.html:
Salvage agents for treatment-experienced patients with resistance act at different entry steps. Enfuvirtide is a fusion inhibitor given by subcutaneous injection. It causes local injection site reactions in 98% of patients, with painful cysts and nodules, and an increased risk of bacterial pneumonia and hypersensitivity reaction. It came out before the integrase inhibitors and is now reserved for resistant virus. Ibalizumab, by contrast, is an IV monoclonal antibody to CD4 domain 2, and fostemsavir is an oral gp120 attachment inhibitor.

This woman with multidrug-resistant HIV takes a subcutaneous peptide that blocks the fusion step, and almost every injection site forms a painful nodule. That is enfuvirtide, and its other specific risk is bacterial pneumonia.
why: Macrocytic anemia is a zidovudine effect.
Fanconi syndrome is a tenofovir DF effect.
Hyperbilirubinemia is characteristic of atazanavir.
Neural tube defects were a historical concern with dolutegravir that updated data do not support.
explain.takeaway: Enfuvirtide is a subcutaneous fusion inhibitor used for salvage that causes injection site nodules in nearly all patients and raises the risk of bacterial pneumonia.
explain.topic: Enfuvirtide and other salvage entry agents
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify administration considerations, adverse effects, and drug interactions for antiretrovirals

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV infection has a viral load of 64,000 copies/mL, CD4 count of 480/mm3, a wild-type genotype, negative hepatitis B serologies, negative HLA-B*5701, and normal kidney function. He wants a single daily tablet. Five tablets are considered.

Which of the following is a complete, guideline-recommended initial regimen?
choices: Lamivudine/zidovudine
Abacavir/lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate
Darunavir/ritonavir/atazanavir
Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir AF
Rilpivirine/efavirenz/tenofovir DF

explain.html:
Monotherapy fails because HIV replicates rapidly and resistance develops quickly, so a regimen needs at least two drugs from different classes. The general approach to initial therapy is a nucleoside backbone of two NRTIs plus an anchor drug: an integrase inhibitor, an NNRTI, or a boosted protease inhibitor. INSTI-based therapy is typically first line because of high potency, low side-effect burden and a high barrier to resistance. The lecture also lists what is not recommended: monotherapy, two NNRTIs, two PIs or two INSTIs, triple NRTI therapy, unboosted darunavir, and emtricitabine with lamivudine.

This man has a wild-type virus, negative HBV serologies and normal kidney function and wants one daily tablet. Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir AF (Biktarvy) is two NRTIs plus an INSTI anchor, a guideline-recommended initial regimen.

OptionBuilt asVerdict

Abacavir/lamivudine/TDF3 NRTIsTriple NRTI, not recommended
Darunavir/ritonavir/atazanavir2 PIs, no backboneNot recommended
Bictegravir/FTC/TAF2 NRTIs + INSTIRecommended
Rilpivirine/efavirenz/TDF2 NNRTIs + 1 NRTINot recommended
why: Two NRTIs without an anchor drug is incomplete.
Three NRTIs with no anchor is triple NRTI therapy, which is not recommended.
Two protease inhibitors with no NRTI backbone is not a recommended combination.
Two NNRTIs in one regimen is not recommended.
explain.takeaway: A complete initial regimen is two NRTIs plus one anchor, preferably an integrase inhibitor, such as bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir AF; never two drugs from the same anchor class or emtricitabine with lamivudine.

explain.objective: Recognize and build a complete ART regimen taking into consideration viral load, patient specific factors and concomitant medications

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old nurse sustains a deep needlestick injury while drawing blood from a patient with known HIV infection and a detectable viral load. She presents to employee health 3 hours later. She is HIV-negative on a rapid test, is not pregnant, and has normal kidney function. She has never taken antiretroviral drugs.

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
choices: Observe and test again in 6 weeks, since needlestick transmission is rare
Start daily emtricitabine/tenofovir DF alone and continue it indefinitely
Give a single intramuscular cabotegravir injection today
Start zidovudine alone for 2 weeks
Start bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir AF for 4 weeks

explain.html:
Antiretrovirals can prevent HIV either before exposure (PrEP) or after it (PEP), with the goal of reducing acquisition after high-risk exposures. PEP covers occupational exposures and non-occupational ones (sexual exposure, injection drug use). It should start within 72 hours and continue for 4 weeks unless the exposure is proven HIV negative. Preferred regimens are complete combinations: bictegravir + FTC/TAF (Biktarvy) or dolutegravir + FTC/TDF, with darunavir/ritonavir + FTC/TDF as the alternative.

This nurse had a deep needlestick from a viremic source and presents at 3 hours, HIV negative, so she is well inside the window. Starting bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide now for 4 weeks is the preferred approach.

RegimensFTC/TDF daily, FTC/TAF daily, cabotegravir IM every 2 months, lenacapavir SC every 6 monthsBictegravir + FTC/TAF, or dolutegravir + FTC/TDF; alternative darunavir/ritonavir + FTC/TDF
why: A significant exposure warrants PEP now, and waiting forfeits the 72-hour window.
Emtricitabine/tenofovir DF alone is a PrEP regimen, and PEP lasts 4 weeks, not indefinitely.
Injectable cabotegravir is a PrEP regimen given every 2 months.
Zidovudine alone is not a PEP regimen; zidovudine is used at delivery and in the infant.
explain.takeaway: PEP starts within 72 hours of exposure with a preferred complete regimen (bictegravir/FTC/TAF or dolutegravir plus FTC/TDF) and continues for 4 weeks.

explain.objective: Recognize goals of pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis and potential therapies for either

questions.stem:
A 35-year-old man with HIV has had an undetectable viral load for 3 years on daily bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir AF. His genotype has never shown resistance. He works rotating overnight shifts and says remembering a daily pill is a constant struggle, though he has managed it so far. He asks whether there is an option that avoids daily pills.

Which of the following is the most appropriate option for him?
choices: Enfuvirtide subcutaneous injections twice daily
Ibalizumab infusions given in clinic every 2 weeks
Cabotegravir injections alone every 2 months
Lenacapavir injections alone every 6 months
Cabotegravir plus rilpivirine injections every 1 to 2 months

explain.html:
Modern ART drugs, especially integrase inhibitors, are potent and have a high barrier to resistance, so some 2-drug regimens are complete. Cabotegravir + rilpivirine (Cabenuva) is given as separate IM gluteal injections by a health care provider every 1 to 2 months, with an optional 1-month oral lead-in to check tolerability. It is approved for switch therapy only, meaning for people already suppressed, and the lecture calls it a great option for patients with adherence concerns about oral regimens. Watch for injection site reactions, hepatotoxicity and depressive symptoms, and avoid CYP3A4 inducers.

This man has been undetectable for 3 years with no resistance and struggles to remember a daily pill around rotating shifts. He meets the switch criteria, so injectable cabotegravir plus rilpivirine fits his problem.

Ibalizumab is IV salvage therapy for multidrug-resistant virus.

Lenacapavir is indicated for treatment-experienced adults with multidrug-resistant HIV, not as solo therapy here.
explain.takeaway: Injectable cabotegravir plus rilpivirine every 1 to 2 months is a complete switch regimen for suppressed patients and helps those who struggle with daily oral adherence.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man has taken a single-tablet regimen of efavirenz, emtricitabine, and tenofovir for 9 years with sustained viral suppression. Routine labs show the following. He also recently had a wrist fracture after a minor fall.

[[labs 0]]

Which change to his regimen is most likely to reduce this toxicity while maintaining suppression?
choices: Replace emtricitabine with lamivudine
Add ritonavir to boost his current drugs
Switch the tenofovir to the alafenamide form
Stop all antiretrovirals until the creatinine normalizes
Replace efavirenz with a second protease inhibitor

explain.html:
Tenofovir comes in two prodrug forms with different toxicity. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) causes renal toxicity, Fanconi syndrome and decreased bone mineral density. Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) is more stable in plasma and stays as the parent compound until it gets into cells, giving about 90% less circulating plasma tenofovir. As a result TAF has less effect on serum creatinine and bone density, though it raises lipids, so a lipid panel should be checked.

This man has glycosuria with a normal serum glucose, low phosphate, proteinuria and a rising creatinine, which is proximal tubular (Fanconi) injury, plus a fragility fracture after 9 years on an efavirenz/emtricitabine/tenofovir DF tablet. Switching TDF to TAF keeps the same antiviral backbone while lowering kidney and bone exposure.
explain.table:
TDFTAF
Plasma tenofovirHigherAbout 90% less
KidneyRenal toxicity, Fanconi syndromeLess effect on creatinine; avoid in severe renal impairment
BoneDecreased bone mineral densityLess effect
LipidsLowerIncreased; check lipid panel
why: Emtricitabine is not causing the kidney and bone injury, and lamivudine with emtricitabine is an antagonistic pair.
Ritonavir raises drug exposures and adds interactions without removing the drug causing the injury.
Stopping therapy invites rebound and resistance when a safer substitute exists.
Two protease inhibitors is not a recommended combination, and it leaves TDF in place.
explain.takeaway: Tenofovir DF causes renal toxicity including Fanconi syndrome and bone loss, and switching to tenofovir alafenamide, with about 90% less plasma tenofovir, reduces these effects.
explain.topic: Tenofovir DF renal and bone toxicity
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify administration considerations, adverse effects, and drug interactions for antiretrovirals

questions.stem:
A 41-year-old man with HIV infection has taken bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide for 2 years. His records show positive hepatitis B surface antigen at diagnosis. He stopped all of his medications 5 weeks ago after losing his insurance. He now has fatigue, nausea, dark urine, and scleral icterus.

[[labs 0]]

Which property of his discontinued regimen best explains this presentation?
choices: Bictegravir chelation of dietary calcium
Mitochondrial toxicity from emtricitabine
Activity of two components against a second virus
Idiosyncratic liver injury from integrase inhibition
Withdrawal of CYP3A4 inhibition by the regimen's booster

explain.html:
Several NRTIs are active against hepatitis B as well as HIV. Lamivudine has HBV dosing, tenofovir DF is approved for HBV, tenofovir alafenamide is approved for HBV as Vemlidy, and emtricitabine carries the same warning. For all four, the lecture flags a severe acute exacerbation of HBV if discontinued, because stopping the drug removes suppression of a virus that is still there. Coinfection with HBV is one of the initial characteristics considered when choosing a regimen.

This man was hepatitis B surface antigen positive and stopped bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide 5 weeks ago. He now has an ALT of 1,240 with jaundice and other viral causes excluded. Two components of his regimen were also suppressing HBV, and the flare followed their withdrawal. In a coinfected patient the regimen must include HBV-active drugs and should not be stopped abruptly.

DrugHBV activity notedIf stopped in coinfection
LamivudineHBV dosing (lower dose)Severe HBV flare
EmtricitabineYesSevere HBV flare
Tenofovir DFApproved for HBVSevere HBV flare
Tenofovir AFApproved for HBV (Vemlidy)Severe HBV flare
why: Chelation lowers integrase inhibitor absorption and does not cause hepatitis after stopping.
Mitochondrial toxicity develops while taking an NRTI, not weeks after stopping it.
Drug-induced liver injury would appear during therapy, not after discontinuation.
This regimen contains no booster, and booster withdrawal would not cause hepatitis.
explain.takeaway: Emtricitabine, lamivudine and both forms of tenofovir are active against hepatitis B, so stopping them in a coinfected patient can cause a severe hepatitis B flare.
explain.topic: Hepatitis B flare after stopping HBV-active NRTIs
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify administration considerations, adverse effects, and drug interactions for antiretrovirals

questions.stem:
A 23-year-old woman with HIV started a single-tablet regimen 4 months ago and has an undetectable viral load. She takes a combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive pill every day without missed doses. She now has a positive pregnancy test. Her antiretroviral tablet contains two NRTIs plus a drug that she was told to take at bedtime on an empty stomach because it can cause vivid dreams.

Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her contraceptive failure?
choices: Inhibition of CYP3A4 raising estrogen levels
Chelation of the hormones in the gut lumen
Induction of CYP3A4 lowering estrogen levels
Competition for renal tubular secretion of the progestin
Antagonism at the estrogen receptor by the NRTI backbone

explain.html:
The NNRTI class shares several traits: no renal dose adjustments, hepatotoxicity and rash including SJS/TEN, drug-specific food rules, and CYP3A4 induction by most members (the exceptions are rilpivirine and doravirine). Induction speeds the metabolism of other drugs and lowers their levels. The lecture calls out the interaction with hormonal contraception, especially estrogen, and recommends progesterone-only methods or a copper IUD instead.

This woman's tablet contains two NRTIs plus a drug taken at bedtime on an empty stomach because of vivid dreams, which is efavirenz. Its induction of CYP3A4 lowered her estrogen levels, and her combined pill failed despite perfect adherence. NRTIs, by contrast, have minimal drug interactions, so the backbone is not the cause.
explain.table:
Drug or classCYP3A4 effectConsequence
Most NNRTIs (efavirenz)InducerLower levels of other drugs, including estrogen
Rilpivirine, doravirineSubstrate, not inducerAffected by inducers
Ritonavir, cobicistatInhibitorHigher levels of PIs and other drugs
why: Inhibition would raise hormone levels and could not cause contraceptive failure.
Chelation with polyvalent cations is an integrase inhibitor interaction and does not involve hormones.
NNRTIs need no renal adjustment and do not interact through renal secretion.
NRTIs have minimal drug interactions and do not act on hormone receptors.
explain.takeaway: Most NNRTIs, including efavirenz, induce CYP3A4 and lower estrogen levels, so progestin-only methods or a copper IUD are preferred for contraception.
explain.topic: NNRTI enzyme induction and hormonal contraception
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify administration considerations, adverse effects, and drug interactions for antiretrovirals

rows.if_right: a boosted regimen (ritonavir or cobicistat) raising levels of a co-administered drug

rows.if_right: an integrase inhibitor taken with a calcium or magnesium supplement

questions.stem:
A 55-year-old man has HIV with resistance to several drug classes after multiple regimen failures. His physician considers adding a drug that binds a host chemokine receptor and blocks viral entry. Before prescribing it, a phenotypic assay is done in which pseudoviruses carrying his envelope genes are tested on two indicator cell lines. Light signal is strong in cells expressing CD4 and CXCR4 and also strong in cells expressing CD4 and CCR5.

Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about the planned drug?
choices: It will work because his virus can use CCR5
It should be avoided because his virus can use CXCR4
It should be given at a doubled dose to cover both coreceptors
It can be used only if he is HLA-B*5701 negative
It will work once combined with a pharmacokinetic booster

explain.html:
Entry can be blocked at several steps: maraviroc blocks the CCR5 coreceptor, enfuvirtide blocks fusion, ibalizumab binds CD4 after attachment, and fostemsavir binds gp120 to block attachment. Maraviroc works only against virus that uses CCR5, so before starting therapy the patient must undergo a tropism test to determine which coreceptor the virus uses, and the drug is for CCR5 ONLY. Its dose depends on CYP3A4 interactions, and it carries a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity.

This man's phenotypic assay shows strong signal in both CXCR4-bearing and CCR5-bearing cells, so his virus can use CXCR4 (dual or mixed tropic). Virus that can enter through CXCR4 simply bypasses a CCR5 blocker, so maraviroc should be avoided. No dose change or booster gives it activity at CXCR4.

Entry agentTargetKey point
MaravirocCCR5 coreceptorTropism test first; CCR5 only
EnfuvirtideFusionSC injection; nodules; bacterial pneumonia
IbalizumabCD4 domain 2IV every 2 weeks; salvage
Fostemsavirgp120 attachmentOral prodrug; multidrug-resistant HIV
why: Some of his virus can use CXCR4 and would escape a CCR5 blocker.
Maraviroc has no activity at CXCR4 at any dose; its dose depends on interacting drugs.
HLA-B*5701 screening applies to abacavir, not maraviroc.
A booster changes drug levels but cannot give maraviroc activity at CXCR4.
explain.takeaway: Maraviroc is a CCR5 antagonist that requires a tropism test first and is used only for CCR5-tropic virus, because virus able to use CXCR4 escapes it.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Identify drug classes of antiretrovirals and understand their mechanisms of action

questions.stem:
A 25-year-old woman asks about preventing HIV. Her male partner has HIV and has not yet achieved viral suppression, and she does not consistently use condoms. Her only exposure is receptive vaginal intercourse. She has normal kidney function. A fourth-generation HIV test today is negative. She asks for a daily oral pill rather than injections.

Which of the following is the most appropriate choice?
choices: Emtricitabine/tenofovir DF daily
Emtricitabine/tenofovir AF daily
Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir AF daily
Dolutegravir/rilpivirine daily
No prophylaxis until her partner's viral load is measured again

explain.html:
PrEP uses antiretrovirals to reduce HIV acquisition in people with ongoing risk. HIV testing is required before starting PrEP to confirm the person is not already infected, and testing is repeated every 2 to 3 months. Four regimens are recommended: emtricitabine/TDF (Truvada) daily for all people with risk factors; emtricitabine/TAF (Descovy) daily, which is not approved for people at risk from receptive vaginal sex because of concerns for effectiveness; cabotegravir IM every 2 months; and lenacapavir SC every 6 months after an oral load.

This woman has ongoing risk from a viremic partner, her only exposure is receptive vaginal sex, she tested negative today, and she wants a daily pill. That rules out the injectables by her choice and Descovy by its approval, leaving daily emtricitabine/TDF.

This is a complete treatment regimen, used for treatment or PEP, not as PrEP.

Her risk is ongoing now, so delaying leaves her unprotected.
explain.takeaway: Daily emtricitabine/tenofovir DF is PrEP for anyone at risk, while emtricitabine/tenofovir AF is not approved for risk through receptive vaginal sex, and HIV must be excluded before PrEP starts.

questions.stem:
A 37-year-old man is admitted with 3 weeks of worsening headache, fever, and confusion. He is newly diagnosed with HIV infection; CD4 count is 22/mm3. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 34 cm H2O, and the cerebrospinal fluid is positive for an encapsulated yeast antigen. Antifungal induction therapy is started today.

Which of the following is the most appropriate plan for antiretroviral therapy?
choices: Briefly defer ART while the acute infection is treated
Start ART today, because all patients start at diagnosis
Withhold ART until the CD4 count rises above 200/mm3
Start only an NRTI pair now and add an anchor later
Never start ART, because his CD4 count is too low to recover

explain.html:
The primary goal of ART is to prevent HIV-associated morbidity and mortality by making plasma HIV RNA undetectable, which also reduces transmission. ART is recommended for all people with HIV regardless of CD4 count, and it can start at the time of diagnosis. A few conditions where deferral may be considered are listed: significant psychosocial barriers to adherence, comorbidities that complicate therapy, and certain acute opportunistic infections such as cryptococcal meningitis. These are assumed to be temporary situations.

This man has newly diagnosed HIV with a CD4 of 22 and cryptococcal meningitis, with antifungal induction starting today. His infection is the example named for deferral, so ART is briefly delayed while the meningitis is treated, then started. Waiting for the CD4 count to recover would never work, since CD4 recovery depends on ART.
why: Starting at diagnosis is the general rule, but cryptococcal meningitis is the named exception for brief deferral.
CD4 recovery depends on ART, so a threshold of 200 would never be reached.
Two NRTIs alone is an incomplete regimen and invites resistance.
ART is recommended for everyone with HIV, and the CD4 count recovers on treatment.
explain.takeaway: ART is recommended for all people with HIV regardless of CD4 count but may be briefly deferred during certain acute opportunistic infections such as cryptococcal meningitis.
explain.topic: When to start ART and when to defer
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Understand goals of antiretroviral therapy and the basis for a complete HIV treatment regimen

questions.stem:
A 27-year-old man received cabotegravir injections every 2 months as pre-exposure prophylaxis; his last injection was 3 months late, and HIV infection is now confirmed. His viral load is 48,000 copies/mL, CD4 count 520/mm3, hepatitis B surface antigen negative, and kidney function normal. A genotype that includes the integrase gene will take 2 weeks. He starts darunavir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir AF today. A student on the team asks why he was not given bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir AF, the integrase inhibitor tablet most new patients in the clinic receive, since integrase inhibitors lower the viral load fastest.

Which property of the chosen anchor drug best justifies the choice in this patient?
choices: It lowers the viral load faster than an integrase inhibitor
It causes fewer metabolic effects, such as dyslipidemia
It has fewer drug interactions because it avoids CYP3A4
It has a high genetic barrier and does not act on integrase
It also treats hepatitis B, protecting the liver if he is coinfected

explain.html:
HIV replicates quickly with an error-prone reverse transcriptase, so drug levels too low to fully suppress replication select resistant variants. Combination therapy pairs an NRTI backbone with an anchor, and the anchor is chosen by what it targets and how hard it is for the virus to escape. Integrase inhibitors are usually first line because they are potent, drop the viral load quickly and are well tolerated, but they depend on an intact integrase target. Protease inhibitors act later in the life cycle, are given boosted with ritonavir or cobicistat, and have a high genetic barrier to resistance; their costs are CYP3A4 interactions and metabolic effects such as dyslipidemia and insulin resistance.

This man acquired HIV during cabotegravir PrEP with a late injection, so integrase resistance is possible and the INSTI genotype is pending. A boosted darunavir anchor does not rely on integrase and is hard for the virus to break, which is why it is the recommended start in this situation even though bictegravir would otherwise be the usual choice.
explain.table:
Anchor classStrengthsCosts
Integrase inhibitor (bictegravir, dolutegravir)Potent, rapid viral load drop, low side-effect burden, high barrier (bictegravir, dolutegravir)Lost if integrase resistance is present; weight gain; cation chelation
Boosted protease inhibitor (darunavir with cobicistat or ritonavir)High genetic barrier to resistance; acts on protease, not integraseCYP3A4 interactions; dyslipidemia, insulin resistance; GI upset
why: Rapid viral load decline is the hallmark of integrase inhibitors, not protease inhibitors.
Protease inhibitors cause dyslipidemia and insulin resistance, so metabolic effects argue against them, not for them.
Darunavir is a major CYP3A4 substrate and cobicistat a CYP3A4 inhibitor, so interactions increase.
Hepatitis B activity comes from the tenofovir and emtricitabine backbone, shared with the bictegravir tablet, and he is HBsAg negative.
explain.takeaway: When integrase resistance is possible, as after HIV acquisition on cabotegravir PrEP, use a boosted protease inhibitor anchor: it targets protease and has a high genetic barrier to resistance.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old woman with HIV and chronic hepatitis B has had an undetectable viral load for 6 years on dolutegravir plus emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. A bone density scan shows osteoporosis, and she had a wrist fracture after a minor fall. Her LDL cholesterol is at goal. Her physician keeps dolutegravir and emtricitabine but replaces tenofovir disoproxil fumarate with tenofovir alafenamide. The patient is anxious because she was once told that stopping her tenofovir could make her hepatitis B flare.

Which outcome is most likely after this change?
choices: HIV suppression is lost because less tenofovir reaches infected cells
Her hepatitis B flares because tenofovir AF has no activity against it
Nothing changes, since both forms give the same plasma tenofovir level
Plasma tenofovir rises, increasing her risk of Fanconi syndrome
Bone and creatinine effects lessen, while her lipids may rise

explain.html:
Tenofovir comes as two prodrugs that differ in where they become tenofovir. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate is converted in plasma, and circulating tenofovir causes its renal toxicity, Fanconi syndrome, and decreased bone mineral density. Tenofovir alafenamide is more stable in plasma and stays as the parent compound until it gets into cells, giving about 90% less circulating tenofovir while still delivering active drug inside the cells HIV infects. Both forms are approved for hepatitis B, and stopping either one can cause a severe hepatitis B flare.

This woman has an osteoporotic fracture on tenofovir DF, so switching to tenofovir AF should lessen the bone and creatinine effects while keeping both HIV and hepatitis B treated, because she is changing forms rather than stopping tenofovir. The trade-off is that lipids rise more with tenofovir AF, so her lipid panel should be checked after the switch.
explain.table:
FeatureTenofovir DFTenofovir AF
Where it becomes tenofovirIn plasmaMostly inside cells
Circulating tenofovirHigherAbout 90% lower
Bone and creatinine effectsDecreased bone density, renal toxicity, Fanconi syndromeLess effect
LipidsLowerIncreased compared with TDF
Hepatitis BApproved; flare if stoppedApproved; flare if stopped
why: Tenofovir AF stays intact until it enters cells, so intracellular activity and suppression are preserved.
Tenofovir AF is approved for hepatitis B, so the swap keeps her hepatitis B treated.
The two forms differ precisely in plasma tenofovir exposure, which is the reason for the switch.
Tenofovir AF lowers plasma tenofovir by about 90%, so kidney toxicity should lessen, not worsen.
explain.takeaway: Tenofovir AF gives about 90% less plasma tenofovir than tenofovir DF, so it spares bone and kidney, still treats hepatitis B, but raises lipids more.
